overview.text: Augusto Pinochet was the Chilean army commander who led the September 1973 coup that overthrew President Salvador Allende. He headed the military government that followed and later held the title of president. His dictatorship dissolved Congress, banned political parties, restricted civil liberties, and committed serious human rights violations. It also introduced sweeping market-oriented economic changes. Opposition grew during the 1980s, and voters rejected an extension of his rule in a 1988 plebiscite. Elections followed in 1989, and Pinochet handed over the presidency to Patricio Aylwin in March 1990. He remained army commander for several more years.

key_facts.text: Pinochet led the coup that overthrew Salvador Allende on September 11, 1973.
His regime dissolved Chile’s Congress and prohibited political parties.
Human rights violations were a defining feature of the dictatorship.
The “No” option won the 1988 vote on continuing his rule.
Pinochet relinquished the presidency in March 1990 but remained army commander.

overview.text: Ramesses II was a pharaoh of Egypt’s Nineteenth Dynasty who ruled for roughly sixty-six years in the thirteenth century BCE. His name appears on monuments across Egypt, and he commissioned temples on a remarkable scale, including the rock-cut Great Temple at Abu Simbel. His armies fought the Hittites at Kadesh in Syria; neither side gained a decisive victory there. Later, Ramesses concluded a peace treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, preserved in Egyptian and Hittite versions. The battle narratives and building projects helped shape his enduring reputation as one of ancient Egypt’s best-known rulers.

key_facts.text: Ramesses II belonged to Egypt’s Nineteenth Dynasty and reigned about 1279–1213 BCE.
His armies fought the Hittites at Kadesh, with no decisive victor.
He made a peace treaty with Hittite king Hattusili III in his twenty-first regnal year.
The Great Temple at Abu Simbel was cut into rock under Ramesses II.
Abu Simbel also includes a smaller temple associated with Queen Nefertari and the goddess Hathor.

overview.text: The Mongol Empire arose from the conquests of Genghis Khan and his successors during the thirteenth century. It became the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching across much of Eurasia. Expansion continued after Genghis Khan’s death, and the empire reached its greatest extent roughly two generations later. Mongol rulers governed diverse settled populations, often retaining local officials for day-to-day administration. Over time, imperial power was divided among major branches: the Yuan dynasty in China, the Chagatai khanate in Central Asia, the Golden Horde in the western steppe, and the Ilkhanate in Iran. These states remained connected by Mongol dynastic origins.

key_facts.text: Genghis Khan forged an empire that became the largest contiguous land empire in history.
The empire was largest about two generations after Genghis Khan.
Four major branches included the Yuan, Chagatai, Golden Horde, and Ilkhanid states.
The Yuan branch ruled China.
Mongol rulers often retained local officials to administer conquered territories.

overview.text: Mikhail Gorbachev led the Soviet Union during its final years and pursued reforms commonly known as perestroika, or restructuring, and glasnost, or openness. His government loosened Soviet control over Eastern European states, helping create conditions for the fall of Communist governments there in 1989. Within the Soviet Union, political changes permitted multiparty elections but also weakened the Communist Party’s hold on power. Hard-line opponents mounted an unsuccessful coup against him in August 1991. As several republics moved toward independence and a new commonwealth formed, the Soviet state unraveled. Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on December 25, 1991.

key_facts.text: Perestroika referred to Gorbachev’s program of restructuring Soviet society.
Glasnost, or openness, was linked to his reform agenda.
He loosened Soviet control over Eastern Europe before the 1989 revolutions.
An August 1991 coup attempt against him failed and weakened his position.
Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on December 25, 1991.

overview.text: A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier of an ancient Greek city-state. The usual equipment included a thrusting spear, a large round shield, and protective pieces such as a helmet, body armor, and shin guards. Hoplites fought in a phalanx: close ranks whose overlapping shields helped protect the men beside one another. This formation made coordinated movement and cohesion especially important. In Athens, the ability to equip oneself for this role was tied to property and civic standing, so hoplite service was also a mark of status. Archers and lighter troops could support the phalanx, rather than every Greek fighter being a hoplite.

key_facts.text: Hoplites were heavily equipped infantry soldiers of Greek city-states.
Their main weapons included a thrusting spear and a large round shield.
A phalanx placed hoplites in close formation with overlapping shields.
Greek armies also used archers and light-armed troops alongside hoplites.

overview.text: Richard II became king of England in 1377 at age ten, succeeding his grandfather Edward III. During the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, he personally negotiated a truce with rebels near London. As an adult he supported art and rebuilt Westminster Hall, but his reliance on favored courtiers and confrontations with powerful nobles created lasting opposition. He later punished rivals, including his cousin Henry of Bolingbroke. In 1399 Bolingbroke returned with an army, removed Richard from the throne, and became Henry IV. Richard died in captivity the following year; historical accounts differ on whether he was murdered or starved himself.

key_facts.text: Richard II reigned from 1377 to 1399.
He inherited the throne from his grandfather Edward III as a child.
He negotiated with rebels during the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381.
Richard rebuilt Westminster Hall and patronized Geoffrey Chaucer.
Henry of Bolingbroke deposed him in 1399 and became Henry IV.

overview.text: Richard III was king of England from 1483 to 1485, near the end of the Wars of the Roses. He was the younger brother of Edward IV and became protector after Edward’s death. Later in 1483 he took the crown from his young nephew Edward V. Edward and his brother disappeared from public view after being placed in the Tower of London; their fate remains uncertain, and Richard’s responsibility is debated. Richard faced growing opposition and was killed when Henry Tudor defeated him at the Battle of Bosworth in August 1485. Henry then ruled as Henry VII, succeeding Richard on the English throne.

key_facts.text: Richard III ruled England from 1483 to 1485.
He became protector after the death of his brother Edward IV.
He took the throne from his nephew Edward V in 1483.
The fate of Edward V and his younger brother remains uncertain.
Richard was killed at the Battle of Bosworth on August 22, 1485.

overview.text: The Third Crusade was a campaign from 1189 to 1192 launched after Saladin, ruler of Egypt and Syria, captured Jerusalem in 1187. Prominent European participants included Richard I of England, Philip II of France, and the Holy Roman emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who died on the journey. Crusader armies captured the port of Acre, while Richard also gained Cyprus. The campaign did not retake Jerusalem, which remained under Muslim control. Its settlement gave European Christian pilgrims access to the city, and Crusader forces held a narrow stretch of Mediterranean coastline. The outcome combined limited territorial gains with failure to achieve the crusade’s central goal.

key_facts.text: The Third Crusade lasted from 1189 to 1192.
It followed Saladin’s capture of Jerusalem in 1187.
Richard I, Philip II, and Frederick Barbarossa participated or set out.
Frederick Barbarossa drowned before reaching the Holy Land.
Crusaders gained Acre and Cyprus but did not recapture Jerusalem.
Saladin allowed European pilgrims access to Jerusalem after the campaign.

overview.text: The Russian Civil War grew out of the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 and continued through the early 1920s. The Bolsheviks’ Red Army fought anti-Bolshevik forces commonly called the Whites, who opposed the new Soviet government. Fighting ranged across a vast territory, including campaigns in Siberia, where Admiral Alexander Kolchak became a prominent White leader. The conflict also involved struggles over control of regions beyond Russia’s central heartland. Red victories against major White armies by 1920 helped secure Bolshevik rule, although warfare did not end everywhere at once. Maps of the war commonly cover events through 1922.

key_facts.text: The civil war followed the Bolshevik takeover of 1917.
The Red Army fought anti-Bolshevik forces known as the Whites.
Admiral Alexander Kolchak was a White leader in Siberia.
Major White armies were routed by the Reds by 1920.
A Library of Congress map series covers the civil war from 1917 to 1922.

overview.text: The League of Nations was created after World War I as an organization meant to encourage cooperation and collective security among states. Its Covenant formed part of the postwar peace settlement, and members registered treaties with the League. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson strongly advocated a league, but the United States Senate did not approve membership, so the country never joined. The League provided a forum for diplomacy and international work, yet it failed to prevent another world war. The organization ended in 1946, transferring its library, archives, and other assets to the newly established United Nations.

key_facts.text: The League was established after World War I under the Treaty of Versailles.
Its Covenant called for international cooperation and peace and security.
Woodrow Wilson advocated its creation, but the United States never joined.
The League published treaties registered by member states.
The League ceased to exist in April 1946 and transferred assets to the UN.
